title: Did Democrats blow it in Florida?
contentHtml:
Eight years ago, Democrats retook the U.S. House, netting 41 seats and winning the national popular vote by 8.6 points in a textbook blue wave. But despite the rosy national environment, Republican Rick Scott narrowly defeated incumbent Democratic Senator Bill Nelson in Florida. In hindsight, that victory, on the heels of Donald Trump’s 2016 win in the state, was the harbinger of a death spiral for Florida Democrats that had begun years earlier.

When I wrote about the Sunshine State back in February, the consensus from both prediction markets and the experts I spoke with was that Democrats were highly unlikely to win the state in 2026. After a decade of losses and underinvestment, it looked like it could take another ten years for Democrats to turn Florida purple again. The short-term goal of the Florida Democratic Party (FDP) was less “win the 2026 Senate race” and more “get out of the superminority in the state legislature.”

But back then, no one knew that 2026 would be a blue tsunami where Democrats would win the national popular vote by 13 points and net nine Senate seats.1 And yet they still lost both statewide races in Florida. Almost immediately, people started posting post-election recriminations that if Democrats had spent more in Florida, they could have pulled off at least one win.

So did Democrats blow a golden opportunity in Florida? Or is the state still too tough a target? That question should weigh on the party because in two short years, Ashley Moody will be up for re-election.
